zones.label: Column 1 running header
zones.note: Lexical review aid: NINJAL, Hideyuki Ohshima and Taichi Aida, Entry Words Data of Nippojisho, version 202510, CC BY 4.0. Source: https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/textdb_dataset/en/nipp/index.html ; license: https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/ . Consulted after independent scan reading; the diplomatic readings and English notes here are reviewer-authored, not an imported transcription.

runs.text: cia. Palaura que ſe poem no cabo das cartas

lines.note: Continues a word and definition from the preceding page: a formula placed at the end of letters. The damaged final letter of cia is read as a, not the OCR's i; the fragment is not expanded.
Completes the description of a self-humbling epistolary formula; this short continuation remains a separate physical row.
The entry identifies a medicinal preparation through a Japanese phrase referring to udo roots. The visible vacane is retained without normalizing the phrase to a modern botanical description.

runs.text: que ſe faz da raiz de hũa erua.

lines.note: Specifies that the medicine is made from an herb's root; hũa retains the printed abbreviation tilde.
The repeated osore expresses apprehensive respect in correspondence. The headword has different marks over its two o vowels, preserved separately.

runs.text: hum moſtra grãde reſpeito no fim das cartas.

lines.note: Completes the epistolary explanation: the writer shows great respect at the end of a letter. The abbreviation grãde is not expanded.
Both Japanese forms denote reverence or worship. The second form's damaged tall letter is read as f, supported by the subsequently consulted NINJAL entry qiǒfai; it is not a repetition of qiǒrai.
Sari and kitaru supply departure and arrival; the Portuguese describes a return or going and coming, not the preceding act of worship.
Vinda completes ida e vinda, the paired motion gloss for kyorai.
The Japanese phrase describes being disordered or mad. Qiǒran replaces the malformed OCR Qibran; Vt introduces its example.
The example means being mad or behaving madly. The tilde over a abbreviates the nasal ending of the preceding headword; no n is supplied in the transcription.
Defines kyorei as an illness involving weakness and cold; the historical medical description is retained without assigning a modern diagnosis.

The gloss concerns years and days passing. The second Japanese form is abraded: qereqi is the provisional visible reading, although the supplied NINJAL index gives qeireqi; no extra i is supplied without secure ink.
As completes the divided Portuguese dias; S marks written usage and is printed upright, separate from the italic gloss.
Repeated sato denotes settlements or villages. The tilde in pouoaçoẽs is retained over e rather than normalized to modern spelling.
Kagami no uchi explains the interior of a mirror. The scan shows a caron over o, like the preceding entry, and an upright written-register label.
Introduces an illness of exhaustion, with the Portuguese word continuing below. There is no secure hyphen after can, so none is added.

runs.text: ſaço, ou falta de vigor, & eſpiritus vitaes.

lines.note: Completes cansaço and describes a lack of vigor and vital spirits. The damaged ending reads vitaes, not OCR vitaos.

runs.text: Hũa eſpecie de etica, ou tiſica.

lines.note: Describes a wasting illness in the source's medical vocabulary. The caron distinguishes this printed headword from Qiorô above; tiſica has no additional j.

runs.text: Qioro. i, Michiuo yuqu, l, ſuguru.

lines.note: Michi wo yuku or suguru means traveling along a road. The Portuguese andar begins at the physical line end.
Completes the travel gloss and begins the saying comparing a lone traveler with a feather. The pilcrow introducing the example is restored from the scan.

Continues the feather comparison; the Portuguese says a lone traveler moves more lightly. The scan appears to print the anomalous cafoxi, where the sense suggests karoshi; the visible tall letter is retained rather than silently changed to r.

runs.text: te anda caminho, & ſe moue que hũa folha.

lines.note: Completes leuemente and the comparison with a leaf or feather. The physical division is retained even though the Portuguese adverb spans two rows.
Describes a book accompanied by explanation and gloss. Groſa is the printed historical form, not a modernization to glosa.
The example describes keeping one's eyes on scriptures and commentaries. The initial pilcrow is visible and restored; the Portuguese translation begins E- at the right edge.

runs.text: ſtar ſempre ſobre os liuros estudando.

lines.note: Completes Estar and explains the example as constant study of books. The source's provisional st allograph in estudando is retained.
Sannuru toshi and kozo both identify last year. Sannuru corrects the OCR's Samnuru; the following Portuguese adjective continues below.
Completes anno passado, the past-year definition. The printed ligature is kept distinct from two separately set long-s letters.
Describes an object used for resting or leaning, glossed as a small supporting bench. The circumflex above the first o is restored from the scan.
Kyotan is directly glossed as a falsehood; this is a complete short entry.
Agetassuru accompanies a definition of granting admission or permission. The Portuguese licença is divided at the physical line end.

runs.text: cença pera algũa couſa, ou dizer, & apreſen

lines.note: Completes licença and adds speaking or presenting something respectfully. Apresen continues below without an invented terminal hyphen.

runs.text: tar algũa couſa a alguẽ falando cõ reſpeito.

lines.note: Completes apresentar and its respectful-address explanation. The abbreviations alguẽ and cõ remain unexpanded; the written-register S is upright.
Akatsuki no sora identifies the dawn sky. The Portuguese places the time before daybreak and divides amanhecer across rows.
Completes amanhecer and supplies madrugada as the early-morning equivalent.
Sannuru fuyu means last winter. The apparent gap after the broad initial Q does not divide the Japanese headword.

runs.text: Moradores do meſmo lugar, ou po-

lines.note: Refers to residents of the same locality. Both o marks are carons; the Portuguese povoação continues below.
Completes povoação, finishing the definition of fellow residents rather than beginning a new word entry.

runs.text: Cidade principal, ou corte del Rey.

lines.note: Defines the capital or royal court. The opening character is the same roman Q used by neighboring headwords, not an italic O.
Describes something easily startled; the example begins a skittish horse. The damaged adjective is eſpantadiça, and the example's o has a circumflex.
Ma completes uma, horse, and the Portuguese confirms the skittish-animal sense. A second example begins hito, a person.

runs.text: Homem que acode com algũs ſubitos na-

lines.note: To completes hito; the Portuguese describes a person who reacts with sudden starts. Naturalmente is divided across this and the next row.
Completes the account of a naturally startled or jumpy person, not a separate sense of the following entry.

runs.text: O errar, ou erro q̃ procede de algũa

lines.note: Introduces error arising from mental disturbance or alarm. The abbreviation q̃ is preserved rather than expanded to que.

runs.text: perturbação, ou noua repentina, ou ruim, &c.

lines.note: Specifies disturbance or sudden, bad news as the cause of the error described above.
Identifies the principal scripture with Hokekyō. The initial i and the v of Portuguese Liuro, both lost in OCR, are visible in the scan.
Completes the source's description by attributing the book to Shaka. Xaca is a Japanese name within Portuguese prose and is printed upright.
Kyōsha is identified as a board-game piece, compared in Portuguese with a horse. Caualo corrects the OCR's spurious internal t; the source's comparison is not replaced with modern game terminology.
Iru ie explains a dwelling or residence. The unmarked o distinguishes the printed form from the preceding game-piece entry.
Describes books and other writings; the damaged middle of the headword is read with the neighboring scripture entries and the supplied lexical index.
Karoku asashi describes something light and shallow or slight. The Portuguese adjective pouca is divided at the right edge.
Completes pouca, followed by the upright written-register abbreviation S.

runs.text: Eſcritura, ou texto que ſe alega, &c.

lines.note: Refers to scripture or a text adduced as authority. The final Japanese t is preserved rather than expanded into another syllable.
The unmarked-o headword means false testimony. The malformed OCR Q uoxet is corrected without transferring the preceding entry's vowel mark.

runs.text: Morada, ou lugar õde hũ eſti.

lines.note: Idokoro denotes one's place or residence. On second-pass enlargement the final type is narrow and dotted, supporting the draft's anomalous eſti rather than the grammatically expected eſtà. The visible i is retained; the damaged word remains a nonblocking reading caveat.
Sannuru aki means last autumn. The mark over final u is preserved as a caron.
Te wo aguru means raising the hands. Aleuantar corrects the OCR's aleuaitar, with the historical u/v spelling retained.
Gives an example involving hand and foot movements and refers the reader to Qiodǒ. Vt and Vide are italic apparatus; the Japanese forms are upright.

Miyako no shū denotes people of the capital. Miyaco occurs inside the Portuguese explanation and appears in the surrounding italic type; it is nevertheless included in the whole-word typeface-review list.
Identifies the religious teacher with Shaka, described as a Buddha so named. The initial is Q, not OCR G; Fotoque is a Japanese term embedded in the gloss.
Sannuru haru means last spring. The opening damaged Q replaces OCR D; the seasonal sequence supports the reading.

runs.text: Qiǒyen. l, Cǒyen. i, Cǒno qemuri.

lines.note: The alternative forms are explained as incense smoke. Chei continues into cheiro below without a supplied line-end hyphen.

runs.text: ro, ou perfume de aguila. ¶ Item, Chei-

lines.note: Completes cheiro and specifies aromatic aguila, followed by a second incense-related sense. The later Chei- has its own visible terminal mark.

runs.text: ro de varias misturas, que ſe poem diante do

lines.note: Describes the scent of mixtures placed before a Buddhist image; the object of diante do follows on the next row.
Fotoque completes the Portuguese explanation of incense placed before a Buddha. It is an embedded Japanese term; S supplies the written-register label.
Kurū saru describes a frisking or unruly monkey, distinct from the preceding incense homograph.
The monkey jumps to and fro; the example begins a reference to treetops. The grave in peralà and the printed word division are preserved.
Completes kozue ni sakebu, crying out in the treetops. The Portuguese begins the same image of a monkey playing and leaping.

runs.text: por cima das pontas das aruores brada, ou faz

lines.note: Continues the treetop scene and says the monkey cries out or makes a commotion.
Traquinada finishes the monkey's noisy antics; the upright S marks the expression's written register.
Age mochiiru concerns taking up, valuing, or admitting something. The Portuguese admitir begins at the line edge.
Completes admitir and adds consenting, finishing the preceding entry's definition.
Refers to funeral observances and supplies a cross-reference. The two vowel marks in each form are preserved rather than made uniform.

Shokyō no aru kura describes a storehouse containing scriptures, glossed as a library. The first headword o is worn; the draft's unmarked reading is retained provisionally although NINJAL supplies a caron.
Tsuyoi yakara identifies forceful people; the Portuguese characterization continues below and is explicitly unfavorable.
Completes the characterization as idle and very bad people, not merely people possessing physical strength.
Describes a scripture desk or stand through the Portuguese comparison with a bench or stool. The doubled zz is preserved.
Specifies that books are placed on the stand; this short row completes the preceding relative clause.

runs.text: Adaga, ou Catana cingida com o gu-

lines.note: Introduces a dagger or sword worn with a particular edge orientation. Cingida corrects the OCR's cinoida; gume continues below.
Specifies an edge directed downward and gives the corresponding Japanese expression. The verb is ſaſu, not the OCR's ſatu.

runs.text: Cingir adaga, ou Catana com o corte pera bai-

lines.note: Translates the preceding expression as girding on a dagger or sword edge-down; baixo is physically divided.
Completes baixo and contrasts another way of wearing the weapon. The source's Darauo is retained as printed.
Finishes the contrast by specifying that the edge faces upward.
Meshi wo kū explains eating rice. This is a new flush-left headword, not an indented continuation of the weapon entry.

runs.text: Eſpelho, ou exemplo bom pera os outros

lines.note: Kikei is a mirror or good example for others. The printed initial aligns with other headwords, correcting the draft's indentation.
Completes the idea of an example to imitate and begins the expression for setting someone up as such an example.
Completes the Portuguese translation as putting forward a mirror and example; the repeated por across rows is preserved.
Defines kike(t) through vital spirits and blood. Its bare final t is retained, and the new-entry indentation is restored.
Gives the principal forms of kiku, to hear, then begins an example about mental quickness. The abbreviated past form is read ijta; its first i is faint.
Completes kokoro or ki no kiita mono, an able and perceptive person. The past-form t replaces OCR i in qijia.

runs.text: Peßoa que tem bom olho pera

lines.note: Mekiki is explained as someone with a good eye for judging things. The printed space in Me qiqi is retained.
Finishes the visual-discernment sense and starts mimikiki, a person with good hearing. The Portuguese person-word is divided.
Completes the good-hearing gloss and introduces ashi ga kiku, referring here to agility of the feet.

Completes the nimble-feet sense, then introduces a woman skilled with her hands. Te qiqi and Molher boa replace garbled OCR; the sentence continues on the next page, while the lower-right cuſture- is a catchword.
